# KeystoneOS Tezino Narrative Project

The Tezino narrative project is a KeystoneOS effort to build a data-driven narrative of an athlete's (Tezino's) physical readiness across a training cycle. As of 2026-06-10 it is in "Phase 1": closing data gaps across force plate (CMJ/IMTP), DEXA, and Catapult sources for summer 2025, before moving to "Phase 2" — building aligned, days-to-camp datasets. On 2026-06-09, a downstream project (`Tezino_CampPrep`) was initiated, using the injury timeline and force-plate history documented in this narrative project as the empirical foundation for an SPC-based live injury monitoring dashboard for Tezino's 2026 summer camp ramp.

## Key Points

- A summer 2025 CMJ backfill (2025-04-01 to 2025-09-10) pulled 2,531 tests / 103,769 metric rows with zero errors and classified 1,108 of them, bringing team-wide coverage to roughly 105 athletes/month through summer 2025; Tezino specifically gained 11 CMJ tests (Apr-Jul 2025), producing refreshed extracts: `tezino_forceplate_raw.csv` (3,264 rows), `tezino_forceplate_classified.csv` (81 tests), and a new `tezino_imtp.csv` (188 rows).
- Root cause of the gap: the VALD sync pages `/tests` by `modifiedFromUtc`; daily syncs only started 2026-01-01 and earlier May 2025 backfills stopped at 2024, leaving a seam in summer 2025 coverage — this was a sync-scheduling artifact, not a pipeline bug.
- Tezino's 2025 summer trend is the inverse of 2024: mRSI dropped from 0.577 (Apr) to 0.518 (Jun) to 0.458 (Jul) to 0.407 ("white tier") on the final test of 7/14/2025 — the worst on record, three weeks before camp — while asymmetry stayed near zero, indicating an output decline rather than a movement-quality regression. This aligns with an IMTP slide from 35-38 N/kg to 23.9 N/kg going into camp, and a 284-lb body-weight nadir.
- Two real testing gaps (not pipeline issues) were identified: no CMJ test in August 2025 despite team-wide testing that month, and no tests at all from 7/14/2025 through April 2026.
- DEXA was dropped from project scope — the data lives elsewhere and is inaccessible, and the available `.mdb` export was demographics-only anyway.
- A Catapult sync attempt failed: the configured OpenField token (minted 2026-05-13) was stale/revoked and rejected as "Unauthenticated" across all hosts and regions, despite appearing otherwise valid.
- **Downstream CampPrep project initiated (2026-06-09):** the injury timeline documented in this narrative project — specifically the 5th MT fracture (2024-07-10, acceleration mechanism, S&C) and the parallel hip strain (July 2025, same mechanism, same window) — became the empirical foundation for `Tezino_CampPrep`, an SPC-based live monitoring project for Tezino's 2026 summer ramp. The mRSI decline and IMTP slide documented in Phase 1 contextualize the injury pattern and inform the baseline and warning-band design for the CampPrep XmR charts.

## Details

The Phase 1 backfill substantially improved data completeness for both the broader team (~105 athletes/month through summer 2025) and Tezino specifically (11 additional CMJ tests plus a brand-new IMTP extract). The findings from this backfill are narratively significant: Tezino's force-output decline through summer 2025, culminating in the worst mRSI on record three weeks before camp, paired with near-zero asymmetry and a matching IMTP and body-weight decline, paints a coherent picture of declining readiness heading into camp rather than an injury-driven movement-quality issue. The database was backed up before the backfill per project convention, and the resulting changes (`docs/DATA-INVENTORY.md`, `docs/NARRATIVE-PLAN.md`, extract script updates) remain uncommitted pending user approval.

Two anchor dates are needed to align Phase 2's days-to-camp datasets: FC25's camp date is provisionally ~7/30/2025, inferred from the weigh-in cadence flipping from weekly to daily on that date; FC24 has no equivalent data signal and must come from the user, with a provisional fallback of ~7/31/2024. The Catapult sync failure is a separate blocker on the Catapult portion of Phase 1 — the immediate next step is generating a genuinely fresh OpenField token (via Settings → API), re-running `auth set-token`, and verifying both the JWT issue date and `auth status` before re-attempting `sync`. This "token looks fine but isn't" failure mode is the mirror image of a credential surprise hit six weeks earlier (2026-04-25) in a different Baylor integration (Perch), where a token that *looked* broken turned out to work fine once the right auth scheme was used — see [[connections/api-credential-assumptions-can-be-backwards]].

The relationship between the narrative project and the downstream `Tezino_CampPrep` monitoring project is one of empirical foundation → live application. The narrative project's historical data analysis (Phase 1 CMJ/IMTP backfill, injury timeline documentation) answers the question "what happened to Tezino before each injury?" The CampPrep project uses those historical findings to design prospective monitoring: the mRSI decline from 0.577 to 0.407 through summer 2025 defines what "the process that preceded injury" looked like, and the XmR warning bands in CampPrep are designed to flag a trajectory toward that state before it is reached in 2026. The two projects are complementary: one is retrospective narrative, the other is prospective monitoring, and both depend on the same VALD ForceDecks and Catapult data sources that Phase 1 worked to make complete.

# Memory Recall Evaluation Harness (30-Question Retrieval Benchmark)

The recall-eval harness is a scheduled benchmark that scores competing memory-retrieval methods against a fixed 30-question set, writing results to `~/.claude/audits/recall-eval/LATEST.md`. On 2026-10-01 a manual run against a freshly built vault index produced the first fully-scoreable comparison of four methods, and its numbers were used to adjudicate whether the Docker/Milvus-backed memsearch stack should be retired in favor of a cheaper alternative. The harness exists precisely so that a retrieval-infrastructure decision is settled by measurement rather than by cost intuition.

## Key Points

- **Four methods, 30 questions (2026-10-01 run):** memsearch 29/30 hit@5, 15 hit@1, 5.7 s; fts5 + Jev 27/30, 19 hit@1, 0.4 s; plain fts5 25/30, 20 hit@1, 5 ms; `rg` 23/30, 11 hit@1, 111 ms. Coverage was 14/14 Tier A notes and 12/13 vault notes.
- **Pre-registered retirement rule:** memsearch is retired only if a cheaper method comes within 1 hit@5. fts5+Jev trails by 2, so the rule did not fire and the Docker/Milvus stack was kept.
- **Recall and ranking diverge.** memsearch wins hit@5 but loses hit@1 (15 vs plain fts5's 20) — it is better at *finding* the right note than at *ranking* it first. A single headline metric would have hidden this.
- **Indexing the vault changed the verdict's availability, not just its value.** Before the overnight index, memsearch was unscoreable; after it (started 22:30, finished 02:49, 259 minutes, 8,302 chunks) it became the best method on recall.
- **The scheduled run failed silently and is not yet diagnosed.** The eval task queued after the index died within ~7 seconds, runs fine by hand, and Task Scheduler history is disabled on the laptop — so the fix is to add output logging to the task before the next Sunday 02:00 run rather than to guess at a cause.

## Details

The harness's value on 2026-10-01 came less from any single score than from the structure it imposed on a decision. The question on the table — keep a Docker/Milvus semantic-search stack or drop to SQLite FTS5 — is exactly the kind of question that gets answered by vibes: the cheaper method is dramatically faster (5 ms versus 5.7 s) and carries no container dependency, and a stopped Milvus container had already caused days of memsearch timeouts (see [[concepts/memsearch-tool-maintenance]]). A pre-registered bar — "within 1 hit@5" — prevented that convenience from deciding the matter. fts5+Jev landed 2 behind, the rule did not fire, and memsearch stayed. This is the same discipline as writing a pass bar before running a model (see [[concepts/pre-registered-pass-bar]]) and the same demand that a model be justified by the failure of the strongest cheap alternative rather than any alternative (see [[connections/measured-baseline-before-model-adoption]]) — here the cheap alternatives were genuinely strong, and the rule was honored in the direction of keeping the expensive tool.

The hit@5 / hit@1 split is the run's most useful substantive finding. Reporting both metrics exposed a behavioral difference the aggregate obscures: memsearch retrieves the relevant note into the top five almost always (29/30) but places it first only half the time (15/30), while plain FTS5 misses more often (25/30) yet ranks precisely when it hits (20/30). Characterized plainly, memsearch is a recall instrument and lexical search is a precision instrument, which argues for using them for different jobs rather than picking one winner. It also means any future retirement test must keep reporting both numbers, since a method that matched memsearch on hit@5 while beating it on hit@1 would be a strict improvement, whereas one that matched on hit@5 alone would be a lateral move.

Two operational lessons attach to the run. First, the overnight index's 259-minute duration confirms that full-library embedding is an hours-scale job belonging to a scheduled task, consistent with the earlier relocation of the heavy reindex into the nightly backup. Second, the eval task's ~7-second death is currently uninformative: it reproduces only under the scheduler, the obvious candidate causes (encoding, a missing API key) were ruled out, and the scheduler's own history is disabled. The chosen response was not a workaround but an instrumentation change — add output logging so the next scheduled failure captures a real error — because an unlogged scheduled job that works by hand supplies no diagnostic surface at all.

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/memsearch-tool-maintenance]] — The tool whose retention this harness adjudicated; its Milvus-container and timeout history is the cost side of the keep/retire tradeoff.
- [[concepts/pre-registered-pass-bar]] — The same practice of writing a numeric bar down before the run, here applied to infrastructure retirement rather than model adoption.
- [[connections/measured-baseline-before-model-adoption]] — The requirement that the strongest cheap alternative actually be measured; this run measured three of them.
- [[concepts/typesafe-api-key-env-vs-file-resolution]] — The misattributed cause of the eval failure, corrected in the same session.
- [[concepts/claude-code-memory-architecture]] — The Tier A and vault material the 30 questions probe.
- [[concepts/automation-stack-doctor]] — The surrounding health-check regime that surfaces failures like the silent scheduled-task death.
- [[concepts/in-session-background-process-limits]] — Why a 259-minute index belongs in a scheduled job rather than a session.

## Sources

- [[daily/2026-10-01.md]] — Windows-laptop maintenance session (17:20): overnight vault index (22:30→02:49, 259 min, 8,302 chunks), four-method 30-question manual eval with hit@5/hit@1/latency figures, retirement rule evaluated and memsearch kept, recall-vs-ranking characterization, scheduled-task ~7-second failure undiagnosed with logging queued as the fix, results committed and pushed to `~/.claude`.

# TYPESAFE_API_KEY: Env-Var vs. File Credential Resolution

On 2026-10-01 a standing claim that `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` was "saved EMPTY" — and the inference that this had caused a scheduled evaluation to fail — was investigated and retracted. The key is present as a real 108-character value in a gitignored file, `C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\typesafe.env`, which the eval reads after finding the Windows *user environment variable* empty. A live Jev call returned 0.11, confirming the credential works. The "saved EMPTY" note in STATUS referred only to the environment variable, not to the credential itself.

## Key Points

- **Two storage locations, one name.** The same credential can live in a Windows user environment variable and in a gitignored dotfile; a tool with a fallback chain reads the file when the env var is empty, so "the env var is empty" does not mean "the key is missing."
- **The status note was true but scoped narrowly, and was then over-read.** "Saved EMPTY" described the env var accurately; the error was treating it as a statement about credential availability and then as the explanation for an unrelated failure.
- **Verified by exercising the dependency, not by inspecting config.** A live Jev call returning 0.11 settled the question that neither the env-var reading nor the file inspection could.
- **The empty env var still matters, but only for a narrower set of consumers:** tools that read nothing but the environment — possibly `TypeSafe_Sandbox` and `42Analytics`. Setting it requires `[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('TYPESAFE_API_KEY','<key>','User')` plus a terminal restart.
- **Downstream correction:** because the credential was never absent, the prior Sunday's Jev run is sound and the key is excluded as a cause of the eval's ~7-second scheduled failure, which remains undiagnosed.

## Details

The session's correction follows a recognizable shape: a recorded observation about one layer was promoted into a diagnosis about a different layer. The observation — that a Windows user env var held no value — was accurate when written. What made it misleading was the compression into "saved EMPTY" in a status file, which stripped the qualifier naming *which* storage location was empty. A later reader, looking for an explanation of a failing scheduled task, found a plausible-looking credential problem and attached it to the failure. Nothing in the status note was false; the qualifier that constrained its scope had been dropped, and a derived conclusion was built on the unqualified version. The remedy was the one that generalizes: go to the owning layer and exercise the actual dependency. A live API call returning a score is a guarantee that neither reading the env var nor reading the file provides, because it tests the whole resolution chain the tool really uses.

The practical residue is a precise statement of which consumers the empty env var affects. Any tool implementing an env-var-then-file fallback — the eval harness among them — is unaffected. Tools that read only the environment, suspected to include `TypeSafe_Sandbox` and `42Analytics`, would fail, and for those the fix is to set the user-scoped variable and restart terminals so running processes pick up the new value. That restart requirement is the familiar Windows constraint that a process's environment is fixed at launch, so a registry-level write is invisible to anything already running. The second consequence is subtractive but equally important: retracting the credential explanation leaves the scheduled eval's failure genuinely unexplained rather than falsely closed, which is what justified instrumenting the task with output logging instead of declaring the issue fixed.

## Related Concepts

# Machine-Scoped Task Execution Rules (Mac-Only Forecast Capture)

Some recurring tasks are bound to a specific machine, and the binding is enforced by the command itself rather than left to the operator's memory. On 2026-10-01 the weekly `/forecast-capture` command was invoked on the Windows laptop and refused per a Mac-only rule established 2026-09-23. The refusal was correct, but it surfaced a verification gap: the newest snapshots on both the laptop and GitHub were dated 2026-09-23, with nothing pushed from the Mac since 9/24, leaving the Wednesday 9/30 capture in an unresolved skipped-or-captured-but-unpushed state.

## Key Points

- **The rule is enforced at the command, not in a convention.** `/forecast-capture` refuses to run on the wrong host, which prevents a duplicate or machine-inconsistent capture instead of relying on the operator to remember where the task belongs.
- **Enforcement creates a blind spot it cannot itself close.** The refusing machine can see only what has been pushed, so a missing snapshot is ambiguous between "not captured" and "captured but not pushed" — two states with different remedies.
- **Urgency came from an external, irrecoverable window, not from item age.** Thursday-night kickoffs overwrite the forecasts, so the pregame state is unrecoverable once games start; the 9/23 snapshot already froze the prior weekend, so nothing was lost *yet*.
- **The remedy was written to be state-conditional:** on the Mac, run `~/DEV/CFB_Victory_Model/scripts/weekly_run.sh` and push before kickoff — or push only, if 9/30 already captured. Explicitly "don't re-run," because a re-run would overwrite a genuine pregame capture with a post-hoc one.
- **The gap was carried as a named per-machine action item** rather than resolved by a workaround on the wrong host.

## Details

A machine-scoped rule trades one failure mode for another, and the 2026-10-01 session shows both halves. On the benefit side, binding the capture to the Mac keeps a single authoritative snapshot lineage and stops the Windows laptop from producing a competing capture whose provenance would be unclear. On the cost side, the host that refuses the command is also the host with the least information about whether the task ran: its only window into the Mac's work is the pushed Git state, and the push itself is a separate step from the capture. When that step lags — nothing from the Mac since 9/24 — the absence of a 9/30 snapshot underdetermines what happened. This is the recurring lesson that confirmation has to come from the layer that owns the work; the laptop can diagnose the symptom but cannot settle the question, so the honest output is an unconfirmed item addressed to the Mac rather than a conclusion.

What made the item urgent was not how long it had been sitting but a counterparty-owned deadline. The forecast-capture pipeline's entire purpose is to freeze pregame probabilities before outcomes exist, since retrodictive figures are optimistic upper bounds rather than out-of-sample grades. Once Thursday-night kickoffs begin, the pregame state for those games is gone and no later action reconstructs it — irrecoverability, not staleness, is the ranking criterion. That same logic shaped the remedy's conditional form. Because a re-run after games begin would produce a snapshot that *looks* like a capture but is contaminated, the action item distinguishes the two live possibilities and prescribes the cheaper, safer branch for each: capture-then-push if 9/30 was skipped, push-only if it was not. Instructing explicitly against re-running encodes the asymmetry — a missing push costs a delay, while an unnecessary re-run silently destroys the thing the pipeline exists to protect.

# Compile Runs That Produce No Articles (Backlog Clearing as Its Own Outcome)

A compile run that extracts nothing is a legitimate and complete result, not a failure. On 2026-10-01 `compile.py` was run to clear a one-log backlog recorded in `.errors.log`; it processed `daily/2026-09-28.md`, created and updated no articles, and left the knowledge base at 191 articles. The run cost $0.98, and the backlog line was then deleted from the error log — the outcome being a cleared queue and a dated judgment that the log held nothing durable, rather than new content.

## Key Points

- **An empty compile has two deliverables:** the backlog entry is cleared, and a judgment is recorded that the source log contained nothing worth keeping. Neither requires an article.
- **The cost is paid for the judgment, not the output.** $0.98 bought a decision about one log; a run that produces nothing is not wasted spend if the alternative is an unresolved backlog or speculative articles.
- **Article count is a health signal, not a target.** The KB holding at 191 after a paid run is the expected result for a thin source log; a compiler that always produced articles would be manufacturing them.
- **The error log is the queue, and must be hand-cleared.** The backlog surfaced as a line in `.errors.log` and only disappeared when deleted after resolution, so the log's emptiness is the indicator that no work is outstanding.
- **Session-level selectivity mirrors run-level selectivity.** The same day's memory flush returned `FLUSH_OK` — the flush tier's equivalent of extracting nothing — showing the same discipline applied one layer down.

## Details

The compiler's value depends on its willingness to produce nothing. If every invocation yielded articles, the knowledge base would accumulate restatements of transient chatter, and the index — which is the retrieval mechanism — would degrade toward noise. A run that reads a log, finds no durable knowledge, and writes no files is therefore functioning as designed, and the appropriate record of it is the build-log entry plus the cleared backlog line. The 2026-10-01 run also illustrates that backlog clearing has standalone value: the `.errors.log` line for the uncompiled 2026-09-28 log was an open item that could not be closed by inspection, only by actually running the compiler and seeing what it found. Paying $0.98 to convert "unknown, possibly unprocessed knowledge" into "processed, nothing there" is a reasonable exchange, and it is the only way to distinguish a thin log from a neglected one.

This selectivity operates at two tiers in the same architecture. The flush tier decides, per session, whether anything from a conversation is worth appending to a daily log, and signals "nothing" with `FLUSH_OK` — which the 2026-10-01 memory flush emitted. The compile tier decides, per daily log, whether anything is worth promoting into articles, and signals "nothing" by leaving the article count unchanged. Both tiers have precedent for the opposite call as well: a flush has retained a no-decisions data snapshot purely on time-sensitivity grounds, annotating its reasoning inline rather than returning `FLUSH_OK`. That the tiers sometimes retain thin material and sometimes discard it is the point — the judgment is per-item, and recording which way it went (by an inline rationale, or by an unchanged count and a deleted backlog line) is what keeps the null results auditable rather than indistinguishable from a silent failure.

# Instrumenting a Silently Failing Scheduled Task

A scheduled job that succeeds when run by hand but dies seconds after the scheduler launches it supplies no diagnostic surface, and on 2026-10-01 that situation was addressed by adding instrumentation rather than by guessing at causes. The recall-eval task, queued to run after the overnight vault index, terminated within roughly 7 seconds; it ran correctly when invoked manually, encoding was ruled out, a suspected credential cause was retracted, and Task Scheduler history is disabled on the laptop. The chosen next step was to add output logging so the next scheduled run — Sunday at 02:00 — captures the real error.

## Key Points

- **Works-by-hand plus fails-on-schedule localizes the fault to the launch environment,** not to the program: the difference between the two invocations is the spawning context, not the code.
- **The diagnostic surface was absent on three fronts simultaneously:** the task emitted no captured output, Task Scheduler history was disabled, and the ~7-second exit left no artifact to inspect.
- **Candidate causes were eliminated rather than assumed.** Encoding was ruled out, and the plausible `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` explanation was investigated and retracted once a live call confirmed the credential worked.
- **The fix is instrumentation, with the failure allowed to recur.** Adding output logging and letting Sunday's scheduled run fail again is cheaper and more informative than a blind workaround, and the recurrence is expected ("the failure will likely recur otherwise").
- **A secondary artifact gap was logged as optional follow-up:** the 02:49 `post-vault-index` rows that never got written to `~/.claude/audits/recall-eval/LATEST.md`, left unopened.

## Details

The asymmetry between a manual run and a scheduled run is itself the primary clue. When identical code succeeds interactively and dies under the scheduler, the variable is the environment the scheduler hands the process: its working directory, its PATH, its user context, its environment variables, and whether a dependency it needs is up at that hour. This project's history supplies several precedents — Task Scheduler's minimal spawn environment requiring full absolute executable paths, and a process's environment being fixed at launch so later registry writes are invisible to it. A ~7-second exit is consistent with that family: long enough to start, short enough to fail before doing real work, which is the signature of a resolution or startup failure rather than a timeout or a logic error. But "consistent with" is not a diagnosis, and the session deliberately stopped short of asserting one.

That restraint matters because a plausible cause had already been wrongly asserted and then withdrawn. The `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` "saved EMPTY" note looked like an explanation, and investigating it properly showed the credential was present in a gitignored file and functional on a live call — removing the candidate and leaving the failure genuinely open. Having lost one false explanation, adopting a second guess would risk the same outcome at greater cost. Instrumentation sidesteps the problem entirely: capture the task's stdout and stderr, let the next scheduled run fail, and read the actual error. The cost is one more week of a non-functional weekly eval; the benefit is that the next failure is self-explaining. The same reasoning covers the unwritten `post-vault-index` rows in `LATEST.md` — recorded as an optional item to investigate rather than reconstructed by inference, since the file itself may hold the partial evidence once opened.

# Connection: Pre-Registered Rules Must Survive Convenient Results

## The Connection

A pass bar written before a run is usually discussed as protection against a *flattering* result — a model that looks good because the bar moved after the numbers arrived. The 2026-10-01 recall-eval run exercised the opposite case. The retirement rule said memsearch would be dropped only if a cheaper method came within 1 hit@5. fts5+Jev finished 2 behind on hit@5 while being roughly 14× faster end-to-end, and plain FTS5 — 5 milliseconds, no Docker, no Milvus container to go down — actually *beat* memsearch on hit@1, 20 to 15. Every convenience argument pointed at retirement. The rule did not fire, and the expensive Docker/Milvus stack was kept.

## Key Insight

A pre-registered bar is only a real constraint if it binds when honoring it is the inconvenient outcome. The three admission conditions in [[concepts/jev-leverage-sweep-typesafe]] and the ≥90%-precision / ≥60%-coverage bar in [[concepts/pre-registered-pass-bar]] were both written to stop a tool from being adopted on enthusiasm; the retirement rule in [[concepts/memory-recall-eval-harness]] stopped a tool from being *dropped* on cost and latency appeal. Same mechanism, opposite direction. The run also shows why the bar's metric choice carries most of the weight: had the rule been written on hit@1 or on latency, it would have fired immediately and a container-dependent stack with documented outage history would have been retired on a metric that measures ranking rather than recall. Choosing hit@5 in advance — before knowing that memsearch would win recall and lose ranking — is what made the decision defensible, and reporting both metrics is what made the tradeoff legible instead of collapsing it into one number that could be read either way.

## Evidence

- 2026-10-01: "Keep Docker/Milvus memsearch. The retirement rule only fires if the cheaper method comes within 1 hit@5. memsearch leads fts5+Jev by 2."
- 2026-10-01: "Caveat: memsearch ranks the right note first less often (15 vs 20), so it's better at finding than at ranking." The cheaper method won the metric the rule did not use.
- 2026-10-01 latency spread: plain fts5 at 5 ms and fts5+Jev at 0.4 s against memsearch's 5.7 s — a convenience gap the rule deliberately ignored.
- 2026-09-22 ([[concepts/pre-registered-pass-bar]]): "≥90% precision when confident / ≥60% coverage on ~40 hand-tagged meetings, written down and labeled before any model run."
- Memsearch's own maintenance record ([[concepts/memsearch-tool-maintenance]]) documents days of timeouts caused by a stopped Milvus container — a standing reliability argument for retirement that the rule, correctly, did not treat as a recall measurement.
